# PART 4 – The result {#part-4-the-result .darkslide background-color="rgba(0,0,0,0)"}

::: {.partlabel}
Part 4
:::

::: notes
The last part runs the final check of the workflow and then reads the result. That check, the sensitivity to the priors, asks whether the result rests on a prior that nobody would defend. Its answer holds the one finding of the module that a report would have to state. Then comes the slope under every model of the session, set beside least squares, and the difference between stating the evidence as a probability and classing it by a threshold. The part closes with the workflow as a whole, in the order in which the session ran it.
:::

## Prior sensitivity {#prior-sensitivity .smaller}

```{r}
#| label: d3-sensitivity
# The sensitivity of the slope and of the persistence to power-scaling of the
# prior and of the likelihood, with the diagnosis of priorsense, whose
# threshold is 0.05 (companion/_model-outputs/bayes_panel_sensitivity.csv)
bayes_sens |>
  datawizard::data_filter(variable %in% c("b_unemp_within", "ar[1]")) |>
  datawizard::data_modify(
    Model = unname(c(common = "One slope", ar1 = "Persistent errors", slopes = "A slope for each country",
                     both = "Country slopes and persistence")[model]),
    Parameter = unname(c(b_unemp_within = "Slope", `ar[1]` = "Persistence")[variable]),
    Prior = fmt_num(prior, 3),
    Likelihood = fmt_num(likelihood, 3),
    Diagnosis = dplyr::if_else(diagnosis == "-", "–", diagnosis)
  ) |>
  datawizard::data_select(c("Model", "Parameter", "Prior", "Likelihood", "Diagnosis")) |>
  tinytable::tt() |>
  tinytable::style_tt(j = 3:4, align = "r") |>
  tinytable::style_tt(fontsize = 0.7)
```

::: {.small}
- priorsense reweights the draws as if the prior, or the likelihood, were raised to a power slightly above or below 1, "a way to check how sensitive the posterior is to perturbations of the prior and likelihood and diagnose the cause of sensitivity" [@KallioinenEtAl2026PriorsenseEfficientPrior, p. 1]
- The slope is insensitive to its prior in every model, between `r fmt_num(min(sens_slope$prior), 3)` and `r fmt_num(max(sens_slope$prior), 3)`. The persistence is sensitive, at `r fmt_num(sens_phi$prior[sens_phi$model == "ar1"], 3)` and `r fmt_num(sens_phi$prior[sens_phi$model == "both"], 3)`: its prior is centred on no persistence, and the data hold a good deal of it
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
The prior stays as it was set before the data, and the conflict is reported. It leaves the slope, the quantity of the claim, untouched, and a report of the persistence for its own sake would have to defend its prior as well as its data.
:::

::: notes
Comparing fits under different priors answers the question of sensitivity for the priors that you compare. The priorsense package asks it for every prior near the one that was chosen, without fitting the model again: it reweights the draws as if the prior, or the likelihood, had been raised to a power a little above or below one, and measures how far the posterior moves. The slope barely moves with its prior in any model, well under the threshold of point nought five, so its posterior is driven by the data. The persistence is another matter. Its prior is centred on no persistence, the data hold a good deal of it, and priorsense reports a potential conflict between the two. [advance] I keep the prior as it was set before the data and report the conflict. The conflict leaves the slope untouched, and it tells us that the persistence, reported for its own sake, would need its prior defended as well as its data.
:::

## The slope across the models {#the-slope-across-the-models .smaller}

```{r}
#| label: d3-slope-intervals
#| fig-width: 9.5
#| fig-height: 2.9
# The slope of the reproduced specification by least squares with 95%
# confidence intervals under conventional and CR2 errors (squares), and its
# posterior median with a 95% credible interval under the four two-way models
# (circles), in points of share per point of unemployment
# (companion/_model-outputs/bayes_panel_summary.csv, the course panel)
tibble::tibble(
  label = c("Least squares, conventional errors", "Least squares, CR2 errors",
            "Posterior, one slope", "Posterior, persistent errors", "Posterior, a slope for each country",
            "Posterior, country slopes and persistence"),
  estimate = c(rep(inference_of("conventional", "b"), 2), common$median, ar1$median, slopes$median, both$median),
  low = c(ci_conventional[[1]], ci_cr2$CI_L, common$q2.5, ar1$q2.5, slopes$q2.5, both$q2.5),
  high = c(ci_conventional[[2]], ci_cr2$CI_U, common$q97.5, ar1$q97.5, slopes$q97.5, both$q97.5),
  kind = c("frequentist", "frequentist", rep("Bayesian", 4))
) |>
  datawizard::data_modify(label = factor(label, levels = rev(label))) |>
  ggplot2::ggplot(ggplot2::aes(x = 100 * estimate, y = label, shape = kind)) +
  ggplot2::geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = "#9aa8b3") +
  ggplot2::geom_errorbar(ggplot2::aes(xmin = 100 * low, xmax = 100 * high), width = 0.25, orientation = "y",
                         colour = ink) +
  ggplot2::geom_point(size = 2.8, colour = ncl_blue) +
  ggplot2::scale_shape_manual(values = c(frequentist = 15, Bayesian = 16), guide = "none") +
  ggplot2::scale_x_continuous(labels = \(x) sub("^-", "−", x)) +
  ggplot2::labs(x = "points of share per point of unemployment", y = NULL) +
  theme_slide(13) +
  ggplot2::theme(axis.text.y = ggplot2::element_text(hjust = 0, colour = "grey20"))
```

::: {.small}
- The model that passes the posterior predictive check, with persistent errors and a slope for each country, puts the average slope at **`r fmt_num(both$median, 5)`**, with a 95% credible interval from `r fmt_num(both$q2.5, 5)` to +`r fmt_num(both$q97.5, 5)`
- Its probability that the slope is negative is `r fmt_num(both$pd, 3)`, and that the slope is steeper than −0.001, a fall of at least one point of share for a rise of ten points of unemployment, `r fmt_num(both$p_beyond, 3)`
:::

::: notes
Here is the slope under every model of the session, in points of share for each point of unemployment. The two squares at the top are least squares: the conventional interval, clearly below zero, and the CR2 interval, which ends at zero. The circles are the four posteriors. The model with one slope sits with the conventional interval, because it shares its assumption. The three models that allow for the dependence all centre a little nearer zero, and their intervals end near zero. The model with both terms, persistent errors and a slope for each country, puts the probability that the slope is negative at ninety-seven and a half per cent, and the probability of a fall of at least one point of share for ten points of unemployment at about ninety per cent. The two approaches agree on the main point: once the dependence of the years enters the analysis, the evidence for a negative slope is much weaker than the conventional fit suggests.
:::

## A probability and a threshold {#a-probability-and-a-threshold .smaller}

::: {.small}
- The CR2 test classes the reproduced specification as not significant at 5%, with p = `r fmt_num(inference_of("cr2_satterthwaite", "p"), 4)` on `r fmt_num(inference_of("cr2_satterthwaite", "df"), 2)` df, a margin of `r fmt_num(100 * (inference_of("cr2_satterthwaite", "p") - 0.05), 2)` of a percentage point
- "only a small change is required to move an estimate from a 5.1% significance level to 4.9%, thus moving it into statistical significance" [@GelmanStern2006DifferenceSignificantNot, p. 328]
- The posterior states the same evidence as a probability that the slope is negative, `r fmt_num(both$pd, 3)`, around a central value smaller than the least-squares slope, and it leaves to the reader the judgement of whether a probability of that size is enough for the claim
:::

::: notes
The two approaches differ in what each makes of that evidence. The test draws a line, and the reproduced specification falls on the side of not significant at five per cent, by four hundredths of a percentage point. Gelman and Stern pointed out how little separates the two sides of such a line: a small change moves an estimate from a significance level of five point one per cent to four point nine. The posterior draws no line. It states the evidence as a probability that the slope is negative, about ninety-seven and a half per cent here, around a central value smaller than the least-squares slope, and it leaves you to judge whether a probability of that size is enough for the claim. In your report this afternoon you state your own result under the errors that you declared, and this is the language for saying what it means.
:::

## The workflow {#the-workflow .smaller}

::: {.small}
1. **Before the data**: priors on scales that can be read, and the prior predictive check
2. **The computation**: R-hat, the effective sample sizes and the divergent transitions of every model
3. **The fit to the data**: posterior predictive checks on a statistic for a grouping that the model leaves out, here the years of a country, and on the bounds of a share. `r if (bounds_both$rep_mean[bounds_both$statistic == "outside"] == 0) "Not one" else "Almost none"` of the replicated cell means of the final model falls outside 0 to 1, and the observed cell means run from `r fmt_num(bounds_both$observed[bounds_both$statistic == "min"], 2)` to `r fmt_num(bounds_both$observed[bounds_both$statistic == "max"], 2)`
4. **The priors again**: power-scaling of the prior and of the likelihood, and a report of any conflict
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
The most direct checks compare simulations with "a summary statistic computed from the data or subgroups of the data, especially for groupings not included in the model" [@GelmanEtAl2026BayesianWorkflow, p. 142].
:::

::: notes
Here is the order in which the session ran the checks, which is the order of the workflow that Gelman and colleagues set out in their book. Before the data, priors that can be read, and a simulation of what they imply. Then the computation, model by model. Then the fit to the data, on a statistic chosen for what the model leaves out, here the grouping of the years by country. The final model also respects the bounds of a share, since not one of its replicated cell means leaves the interval from nought to one. And then the priors again, with power-scaling. [advance] The failed posterior predictive check did the most work of the four, because both of the models that followed it, the persistent errors and the slope for each country, were readings of its failure. A posterior is worth reading once all four steps have passed, and a report says what each of them found.
:::
